transcript:
Live from NPR News, I'm Dale Willman.
The Supreme Court has blocked the use of a Missouri congressional map backed by President
Trump.
It's a setback to Republican efforts to keep control of the House of Representatives.
St. Louis Public Radio's Jason Rosenbaum reports.
The High Court stayed an appeals court decision that required Missouri to use a map aimed
at ousting Democratic Congressman Emanuel Cleaver.
Instead, Missouri voters will use congressional lines passed four years ago that include a
safe seat for Cleaver.
Missouri Republicans targeted Cleaver at the behest of Trump to prevent the GOP from losing
control of the House, but redistricting opponents gathered enough signatures to prevent the
Trump-backed map from going into effect.
Republicans hold a slim majority in the U.S. House, so barring any more rulings in what
has been a process with many turns, the ruling could help Democrats win control of the chamber.
For NPR News, I'm Jason Rosenbaum in St. Louis.
The number of U.S. troops who've died or been wounded in the Iran War continues to rise,
as NPR's Quill Lawrence reports 19 service members have now died and 861 others have
been wounded.
18 U.S. troops have died in combat since the war began in February, and this week the Army
announced an additional officer died, not in combat, after she fell ill on a flight
toward the region.
The number of wounded in action has also crept up, including a number of traumatic brain
injuries that can take weeks to diagnose.
The Pentagon has said that most of the wounded have been able to return to duty.
The strain of long deployments is also taking a toll.
While President Trump initially and repeatedly said the war would be over in days or weeks,
it has included a record-breaking nine months at sea for the Abraham Lincoln Carrier Group,
which is now en route home.
The Navy confirmed this week that at least eight sailors attempted suicide during that
tour.
Quill Lawrence, NPR News.
A powerful nor'easter is expected to hit parts of the east coast this weekend with heavy
rain and high winds.
Ocean State Media's David Wright has more from Rhode Island.
Nor'easters tend to be winter events here in New England.
It's a storm much like a hurricane, except that it doesn't come up from the tropics.
This one is forecast to linger for days, Sean Lacy, town manager in Westerley, Rhode Island,
is urging residents to batten down the hatches.
You're going to get a lot of rain, you're going to get wind.
If you have outside patio furniture, try and secure it or bring it inside.
Do everything you can to secure the items in your yard as you would any other type of
wind event storm.
Power outages are expected too, as gale force winds topple trees.
All foliage hasn't really begun yet, so those trees full of leaves are even more vulnerable
to the storm.
For NPR News, I'm David Wright in Westerley, Rhode Island.
A drop in oil prices helped to calm Wall Street on Friday.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed up 0.93 percent, the NASDAQ closed up 0.48 percent.
You're listening to NPR News.
The U.S. is ending funding for Zimbabwe's health programs next week after the country
rejected a U.S. deal that required the country to share sensitive health data.
The country has been a major recipient of U.S. health aid for HIV, tuberculosis and malaria
programs.
There are concerns that the country will be unable to independently replace that funding.
New polls out this week paint a mixed picture of how people feel about AI.
As NPR's Windsor Johnston reports, the surveys come as calls continue from industry leaders
to slow development of the rapidly changing technology.
New Reuters' Ipsos poll found 73 percent of Americans worry that AI companies are not
doing enough to prevent serious harm.
Harvard Medical School psychologist Luanna Marquez says those concerns make sense, but
people need a way to stay informed about the risks of AI without getting overwhelmed by
every warning.
I think you're looking at data in a balanced way, trying to take your emotions out and
not drinking out of a fire hose.
I think if you're every day and go, "What's happening to AI today?" you're basically
activating that threat in your brain.
In a separate Gallup poll, 34 out of 37 countries surveyed said they feel optimistic about AI,
but three out of four Americans told Gallup AI worries them.
Windsor Johnston, NPR News.
The Irish Band U2 is back in school today to surprise students at Mount Temple Comprehensive
School in Dublin with a seven-song concert.
The band was formed at the school 50 years ago.
Lead singer Bono joked with the students, saying the band had escaped from the science
lab.
The visit was a promotion for the band's newest album.
I'm Dale Willman, NPR News.
This message comes from Angie.
